policy_title: Introduce a Fair Politics Act and reform democracy
stated: Introduce a Fair Politics Act to strengthen democracy by repealing the Elections Act 2022, restoring Electoral Commission powers, replacing first-past-the-post with proportional representation, introducing state funding for political parties, and removing the cap on Electoral Commission fines. It also commits to replacing the House of Lords with an elected second chamber, giving 16 and 17-year-olds the right to vote and stand for election, and introducing residence-based voting rights.

source.quote: Elected Greens will introduce a Fair Politics Act to strengthen our democracy now. This legislation would do the following: • Repeal the anti-democratic Elections Act 2022, ending the need to provide voter-ID. • Restore the Electoral Commission’s power to prosecute, and abolish the barriers to third-party campaigning so that all groups can be transparently involved in the democratic process. • Replace the first-past-the-post system for parliamentary and council elections with a fair and proportional voting system. • Introduce a fair system of state funding for political parties to eliminate dependence on large private donations. • Remove the cap on fines that can be imposed by the Electoral Commission on political parties that have been found to have breached electoral law. Our priorities will be: • Replacing the House of Lords with an elected second chamber. • Votes for 16-year-olds and residence-based voting rights. • Give 16 and 17-year-olds the right to vote and to stand for parliament and other elected offices.

bearing_set.reason: The policy directly and substantively changes voting rights (16/17-year-olds, residence-based), the electoral system (FPTP→PR), democratic oversight bodies (Electoral Commission powers and fines), party funding rules, and the composition of the legislature (elected Lords) — all core O9 indicators of democratic and voting rights.

membership_note: This is a single-target democratic-reform package whose real verdict lands entirely on O9 (voting and democratic rights). State funding for parties would carry a public cost, but relative to total public expenditure the sum is almost certainly negligible for O12. Downstream effects of PR on policy outcomes are too speculative and indirect to pin to any other fundamental's specific indicator; they do not clear the non-negligible bar.
